How tidal locking works

A moon is tidally locked when it takes as long to rotate once on its axis as it takes to orbit its planet once. The Moon is the nearest example, which is why the same face always points toward the Earth.

The lock forms because the planet's gravity pulls harder on the near side of the moon than on the far side. The resulting bulge is dragged out of line while the moon spins, and the pull on it slows the spin until the bulge stays under the planet.

How long it takes

The time to lock depends on the moon's distance, its size and how rigid it is. A large moon close to its planet locks within a few million years, while a small one far away may take longer than the age of the universe.
